question: Pilates vs Strength training for Lower back pain
search_summary: Europe PMC: 3 searches, 40 new records screened, 6 suggested. Answer uses checked cards only. AI-checked, not clinician-reviewed.

pico.p: People with lumbar low back pain

gaps: 1 of 6 papers found were not read: no free full text, or held by a check.
No true head-to-head trial of Pilates versus pure strength training in the same low back pain population.
Most evidence is in chronic nonspecific low back pain, not acute, postpartum, athlete, or older adult cases.
Follow-up is usually short-term; long-term recurrence, adherence, and return-to-sport remain unclear.

answer.answer: No clear winner in chronic nonspecific low back pain: Pilates and strength-type core training both help, but neither is proven superior. Biggest caveat: evidence is mostly indirect to generic strength training and very heterogeneous, with non-significant subgroup differences.
actions: Use core training when exercise is appropriate for chronic nonspecific low back pain.
Do not switch to Pilates solely to improve pain over strength training.
Do not switch to core resistance solely to improve disability over Pilates.
Set expectations around short-term gains rather than proven long-term durability.
If choosing core regimens, consider eight or more weeks; shorter programmes looked less convincing.
Progress using pain, disability, and tolerance rather than assumed modality superiority.

comparison.title: Core training helps pain and function
comparison.design: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
comparison.finding: Pain SMD 1.03 and ODI SMD -0.70 versus control; Pilates/resistance subgroup differences were not significant.

comparison.title: Core training for chronic low back pain: modest pooled benefit, very …
comparison.design: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
comparison.finding: Across active regimens, pain SMD -0.56 and function SMD -0.81; no best core method identified.

comparison.title: Core training may help chronic low back pain, but heterogeneity is high
comparison.design: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
comparison.n: Adults with chronic non-specific low back pain, 33 RCTs
comparison.finding: Overall pain SMD −0.95 and function SMD −1.09; best modality unclear, Pilates function crossed no effect.

agreement: All reviews support exercise-based core training over control for short-term pain or function in chronic nonspecific low back pain.
Reviews mentioning Pilates and resistance-type options did not confirm a superior modality.
Heterogeneity was high or very high across studies.
conflicts: Numerical winners differed: Pilates for pain in one review, core resistance for ODI in one, SET in another.
Pilates function ranged from favourable pooled rankings to crossing no effect, likely from mixed comparators and scales.
Active-comparator pooling favoured experimental regimens overall, but could not show whether Pilates or strength work drove the effect.
